report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: College students encounter academic hurdles such as failing exams or missing goals.
The Motivational Theory of Life-Span Development outlines goal engagement, goal adjustment, and self-protection control strategies for regulating behavior after setbacks.
We examined profiles of intended control strategy use after midterms in difficult courses, and their predictors and outcomes.
We identified four student profiles: Low, Medium, High, and Engaged Strategy.
Lower midterm performance predicted membership in the High and Engaged Strategy profiles.
Engaged Strategy students (high goal engagement, low goal adjustment and self-protection) outperformed High Strategy students and, in most quarters, Medium Strategy students in final course grades.
High Strategy students (high engagement, goal adjustment, and self-protection) had the lowest final course grades.
Both High and Engaged Strategy students reported more positive feelings than others, but High Strategy students also reported more negative feelings than Low Strategy students.

Findings suggest that focusing on goal engagement after a setback is more adaptive than combining it with goal adjustment and self-protection, and that students need support in identifying adaptive strategies.
College students face a multitude of academic challenges as they become primary agents of their own education.
Compared with high school, college offers far greater freedom for students to structure their own learning activities and environments.
Against this background, the ability to self-regulate goals and behaviors becomes particularly critical when students encounter difficulties in challenging courses.
Successfully navigating such obstacles is essential not only for academic success, but also for students' psychological well-being (Adlaf et al., 2001; Hussain et al., 2013).

text.text: The Motivational Theory of Life-Span Development (MTD; Heckhausen et al., 2010 Heckhausen et al., , 2019;; Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995) provides a framework for understanding how individuals respond to such challenges.
text.formatted: The Motivational Theory of <ref type="bibr">Life-Span Development (MTD;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Heckhausen et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Heckhausen et al., , 2019;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995)</ref> provides a framework for understanding how individuals respond to such challenges.

text.text: The theory outlines a range of control strategies that individuals use to engage with, adjust, or disengage from their goals when they face obstacles.

When college students receive a disappointing midterm exam grade in a difficult course, for instance, they may persist through goal engagement strategies (e.g., increasing effort or seeking help), lower their aspirations through goal adjustment strategies, or protect their selfesteem through self-protection strategies (e.g., reminding themselves that others are struggling too).

In the present study, we examined how students combine these strategies, and whether some combinations of control strategies are better suited than others to help students succeed in challenging courses while maintaining their well-being.
We applied latent profile analysis (LPA) to data from 1,338 undergraduate students in their most difficult course across three consecutive academic quarters.

We identified profiles of students' intended control strategy use after midterm exams, examined how midterm performance and course-specific motivational beliefs predicted profile membership, and tested whether the profiles differed in final course grades and psychological well-being.
MTD posits that individuals use a repertoire of control strategies to adapt to opportunities and constraints in their environment.

Although the theory was originally developed in the context of broader developmental goals across adulthood (e.g., career and family goals), it has been extended to educational goals to understand how learners respond to challenges in learning environments (e.g., Hamm et al., 2019; von Keyserlingk et al., 2022).

text.text: In the context of a challenging college course, students can respond to setbacks with four types of strategies.

Goal engagement strategies involve actively pursuing the goal, for example by increasing study time and effort, seeking help from peers or counselors when one's own skills or resources are insufficient, or sustaining one's motivation by anticipating success or avoiding distractions.
Goal adjustment strategies involve revising the goal itself, such as lowering one's grade aspirations for the course to a more attainable level.

Selfprotection strategies involve buffering the threat that setbacks pose to one's self-esteem and confidence, for example by attributing failure to external factors or by reminding oneself that others are struggling as well.
Whereas goal adjustment changes the goal, self-protection leaves it intact and protects the motivational resources needed for further goal pursuit.
Goal disengagement strategies involve abandoning the goal altogether (e.g., withdrawing from the course).

Central to the theory is the congruence principle: goal engagement is adaptive when goals remain attainable despite setbacks, whereas goal adjustment and disengagement become adaptive when goals are unattainable or excessively costly (Heckhausen et al., 2010 (Heckhausen et al., , 2019)).

text.text: Accordingly, no single strategy is adaptive by itself; its value depends on the situation and on the other strategies a student uses alongside it.
According to MTD, control strategy use depends on two characteristics of a goal: its desirability and its attainability (Heckhausen et al., 2010).

text.text: Individuals tend to engage with goals that are desirable and attainable and to adjust or disengage from goals that are not.
Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT; Eccles et al., 1983; Eccles & Wigfield, 2020) offers a way to capture these goal characteristics in a college course.
text.formatted: Situated <ref type="bibr">Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Eccles et al., 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref> offers a way to capture these goal characteristics in a college course.

text.text: Expectancies for success, i.e., students' beliefs about how well they will perform in an upcoming task, reflect the perceived attainability of doing well in a course.
Subjective task values, which comprise the attainment, intrinsic, and utility value as well as the perceived cost of a task, reflect the desirability of doing well in a course.

These motivational beliefs are key drivers of students' engagement and performance: students with higher expectancies and values show greater course engagement (e.g., Trautwein et al., 2012; Wolters et al., 2013; Wu & Fan, 2017) and better course performance (e.g., Fan & Dempsey, 2017; Wang & Liou, 2018; Wu et al., 2020).

text.text: Von Keyserlingk et al. (2022) examined how these beliefs and students' midterm exam experiences relate to their intended control strategy use after a midterm exam in a difficult college course.

text.text: Students with higher subjective task values intended to use more goal engagement, goal adjustment, and self-protection strategies, which aligns with the MTD's assumption that individuals commit to desired and valued goals.
The authors interpreted the higher use of goal adjustment among these students as adaptive recalibration of overambitious goals.
Students with higher ability beliefs intended to use fewer goal adjustment strategies, which aligns with the MTD's assumption that individuals keep their goals when they are generally attainable.
Students who perceived their midterm exam as more difficult than expected intended to invest more effort and to adjust their grade aspirations.

These associations held mainly for students with low or average subjective task values, whereas students with high values planned high levels of effort and adjustment regardless of their exam experience.
These findings suggest that students do not rely exclusively on either goal engagement or adjustment, particularly after a setback, but may combine them in different ways.

Whereas expectancies reflect perceived attainability, performance feedback provides objective information about it and may also shape students' control strategy use. Hall (2008) found that poorer test grades predicted a shift in students' relative emphasis toward positively reinterpreting their negative experiences, a strategy conceptually related to self-protection.

text.text: Taken together, prior research suggests that both motivational beliefs and performance feedback are associated with students' control strategy use.
However, this evidence is limited in two ways.
First, objective performance feedback has not been examined alongside motivational beliefs.

Von Keyserlingk et al. (2022) assessed exam difficulty relative to students' prior expectations, which is not equivalent to poor performance: a student with low expectations who performs poorly may still rate the exam "as expected." Hall (2008) examined grades but not motivational beliefs as predictors of control strategy use.

text.text: Second, both studies examined strategies separately and thus cannot show which combinations of strategies students adopt.
Examining how midterm performance and motivational beliefs predict profiles of control strategy use can address these gaps.

text.text: In the following, we review evidence on how control strategies relate to academic performance and psychological well-being.
Goal engagement strategies generally predict academic success.
Students who planned to invest more time and effort in their studies obtained higher course grades, beyond their prior achievement (Hamm et al., 2013).

text.text: Goal engagement strategies that sustain motivation, such as reminding oneself why one's education matters, anticipating success, or avoiding distractions, did not directly predict grades but predicted greater effort investment months later, which in turn predicted higher grades (Hamm et al., 2013).

text.text: These motivation-sustaining strategies also appear to protect well-being: among students with low high school grades, they predicted fewer depressive symptoms, indirectly through greater effort investment and more favorable emotions about their course performance (Hamm et al., 2015).

text.text: Person-centered research further suggests that investing time and effort may be particularly important. Han et al. (2018) identified profiles of first-year students based on three learning strategies: time management, self-regulated learning, and goal engagement (i.e., investing time and effort in one's academic goals).

text.text: Students high in goal engagement but only moderate in the other two strategies earned writing course grades and credits comparable to those of students high in all three strategies, although their first-semester GPA was lower.
Evidence on self-protection strategies is more mixed.

In one study, positively reinterpreting academic experiences, a strategy conceptually related to self-protection, negatively predicted final course grades and GPA after accounting for prior achievement and other motivational factors (Daniels et al., 2014).

text.text: In another study, the benefits of selfprotection strategies depended on students' initial performance (Hall, Perry, et al., 2006).

text.text: Among students who had performed poorly on their first course test, those who reported more positive reinterpretation and comforting social comparisons felt happier and prouder about their course performance.

Those who combined these strategies with a strong sense of control also achieved higher cumulative GPAs, withdrew from fewer courses, and reported less general stress and regret than those who relied on a sense of control alone.
Among students who performed well, these self-protection strategies showed no such benefits.
Positive reinterpretation was also associated with lower perceived stress among female but not male students (Hall, Chipperfield, et al., 2006).

text.text: To our knowledge, evidence on goal adjustment and academic performance or wellbeing in college remains scarce.

Taken together, prior research suggests that the benefits of control strategies depend on students' initial standing and on how strategies are combined, with self-protection appearing most beneficial for struggling students with a strong sense of control.
However, these studies examined at most two strategies at a time and did not include goal adjustment.

Therefore, it is unclear whether self-protection is similarly beneficial when combined with goal engagement or goal adjustment, and more generally, whether profiles of goal engagement, goal adjustment, and self-protection strategies differ in their associations with achievement and psychological well-being.
According to MTD, control strategies are a central process through which individuals regulate their motivation and behavior during goal pursuit (Heckhausen et al., 2010).

text.text: Prior research has linked control strategies to college students' academic performance and psychological well-being, but the findings are mixed.
The benefits of a given strategy appear to depend on students' initial performance and on the other strategies they use (Hall, Perry, et al., 2006).

text.text: However, prior studies examined strategies separately or in pairs, using variablecentered analyses that cannot show which strategies students combine.
With the present study, we aim to improve our understanding of adaptive combinations of control strategy use in relevant and naturalistic contexts.
We used longitudinal data from 1,338 undergraduate students across three academic quarters.
Students reported their intended control strategy use after receiving their midterm grades in the course they considered most difficult.
Because very few students withdrew from their most difficult course, we focused on goal engagement, goal adjustment, and self-protection and did not examine goal disengagement.
We applied latent profile analysis (LPA), a person-centered approach that identifies subgroups of students with similar patterns of use (Spurk et al., 2020), to address three research questions.

We used a subsample of students who completed short weekly online surveys across the academic year.

Our sample (N = 1,338) consisted of three cohorts of students (academic years 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23) who completed at least one survey on intended control strategy use across three quarters (fall n = 964; winter n = 833; spring n = 655).

At the end of each quarter, after receiving their final course grades, students reported positive and negative feelings they experienced throughout the quarter.

Intended Control Strategy Use.
Ten items assessed how students planned to use control strategies to improve their course performance (Table 1).

text.text: All items started with the prompt "Thinking about the next exam in your difficult course [course name], how likely is it that you will…?"

Six items assessed goal engagement strategies (e.g., "increase your effort and time invested in this course," "get help from classmates or friends," "try to stay away from anything that could distract you from your course work"), two items assessed goal adjustment strategies (e.g., "adjust your grade aspiration for this course"), and two items assessed self-protection strategies (e.g., "remind yourself that other students are struggling too in this course").
Students responded on a 7-point scale from 1 (not at all likely) to 7 (extremely likely).
The research team developed the items based on the MTD literature (Heckhausen et al., 2010 (Heckhausen et al., , 2019;; Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995).

Students' self-reported midterm exam grades were converted to a numerical scale from 0 (F) to 12 (A+).
Three items were used to assess how students perceived their performance in their most difficult course, as an operationalization of expectancies for success.
One example item is "Over the last few weeks, how good have you been in learning new things in your most difficult course [course name]?"

Six items in total were used to assess students' subjective task values in their most difficult course, with two items each devoted to utility, intrinsic, and attainment value of the course.
All items started with the prompt "Based on your experiences in this course, how much is your most difficult course [course name]…?"
Example items are "interesting to you" (intrinsic value), "useful in terms of your long-term goals" (utility value), and "important to your academic identity" (attainment value).
Students responded to these items on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely).

Final Course Grades.
Students' official final course grades were converted to a numerical scale from 0 (F) to 12 (A+).
Sixteen items assessed students' general psychological well-being during the quarter: positive feelings (nine items) and negative feelings (seven items).
All items started with the prompt "How often in the last term have you felt…?"

Two example items for positive feelings are "happy with your academic activities" and "well supported emotionally," and two example items for negative feelings are "anxious about your academic performance" and "worried about making friends."
Students responded to these items on a slider scale from 0 (never) to 100 (all of the time).
The research team developed the items.

In this study, we examined profiles of college students' intended control strategy use after a midterm exam in their most difficult course, their predictors, and their associations with final course grades and psychological well-being.
We identified four profiles: High, Medium, Low, and Engaged Strategy.

Students with lower midterm grades and higher subjective task values were more likely to be in the High or Engaged Strategy profile, i.e., to intend to use all strategies or goal engagement strategies at high levels.

Despite lower midterm grades, students in the Engaged Strategy profile attained higher final course grades than students in the High Strategy profile and, in two of three quarters, the Medium Strategy profile, whereas students in the High Strategy profile obtained the lowest grades and reported both more positive and more negative feelings.

The Engaged Strategy profile aligns with the theoretical proposition that goal engagement strategies tend to function together, such that individuals mobilize several means to reach a goal, for example by increasing their effort and avoiding distractions (Heckhausen et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The Engaged Strategy profile aligns with the theoretical proposition that goal engagement strategies tend to function together, such that individuals mobilize several means to reach a goal, for example by increasing their effort and avoiding distractions <ref type="bibr">(Heckhausen et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The High Strategy profile, in contrast, combined high goal engagement with goal adjustment and self-protection.
This pattern is consistent with the finding that students intend to invest more effort and adjust their aspirations at the same time after a setback (von Keyserlingk et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with the finding that students intend to invest more effort and adjust their aspirations at the same time after a setback (von <ref type="bibr">Keyserlingk et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In our sample, no profile combined goal adjustment or selfprotection with low goal engagement.
A possible explanation is that students at the studied competitive research university may be reluctant to lower their aspirations without also working harder.
Notably, students in all profiles were less likely to endorse seeking help from counselors or academic resource centers and attributing their struggles externally than other strategies.
In a high-achieving environment, acknowledging difficulties and seeking help may be stigmatized, and students may feel pressured to solve problems on their own.
Indeed, students are more likely to seek help in supportive, mastery-oriented than in performanceoriented learning environments (Karabenick & Gonida, 2017).
text.formatted: Indeed, students are more likely to seek help in supportive, mastery-oriented than in performanceoriented learning environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Karabenick & Gonida, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Students with higher midterm grades were more likely to be in the Low or Medium Strategy profile, suggesting they saw little need to change their approach (i.e., to increase effort or adjust goals) because they were already performing well.
Students with lower midterm grades were more likely to be in the High or Engaged Strategy profile and thus intended to use all strategies, or goal engagement strategies specifically, at high levels.
This aligns with MTD that individuals use control strategies to mobilize effort or adjust their goals in the face of obstacles and setbacks (Heckhausen et al., 2010).
text.formatted: This aligns with MTD that individuals use control strategies to mobilize effort or adjust their goals in the face of obstacles and setbacks <ref type="bibr">(Heckhausen et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: It also echoes the finding that students who perceived the midterm exam as more difficult than expected intended to invest more effort and adjust their aspirations (von Keyserlingk et al., 2022) and extends it by showing that students' intended strategy use responds to objective performance feedback.

text.text: Students with higher subjective task values were more likely to be in the High and Engaged Strategy profiles, and students with lower values were more likely to be in the Low Strategy profile.

This is consistent with SEVT's proposition that students who find a course interesting, useful, or important invest more in it (Eccles et al., 1983; Eccles & Wigfield, 2020): students who valued the course more intended to increase their effort after a setback and stay committed to the course.

text.text: The fact that higher values also predicted membership in the High rather than the Engaged Strategy profile in two quarters is consistent with the finding that students who value a course also report more goal adjustment, which may reflect the recalibration of overly ambitious goals (von Keyserlingk et al., 2022).

text.text: Contrary to our hypothesis, ability beliefs were largely unrelated to profile membership; the only effect, in fall, indicated that students with higher ability beliefs were more likely to be in the High than in the Low or Medium Strategy profile.
In the present study, ability beliefs were assessed as students' perceived performance over the past few weeks rather than their expectations for future exams.

Given their substantial correlation with midterm grades (rs = .58 to .62), midterm grades, a more objective indicator of performance, may have overshadowed ability beliefs as a predictor of intended control strategy use.

Among the control variables, female and underrepresented minority students were somewhat more likely to be in the High Strategy profile, but these effects were inconsistent across quarters and should be interpreted with caution.

The Engaged Strategy profile was associated with higher final course grades than the High Strategy profile in all quarters and than the Medium Strategy profile in two quarters, consistent with findings that goal engagement strategies predict academic success (Hamm et al., 2013; Han et al., 2018).

text.text: Students in both the Engaged and High Strategy profiles reported more positive feelings than students in the Low and, in most quarters, the Medium Strategy profile, but students in the High Strategy profile also reported more negative feelings than those in the Low Strategy profile.

The Engaged Strategy profile thus appears to be the most adaptive: despite lower midterm grades than students in the Low and Medium Strategy profiles in most quarters, these students attained the most favorable academic and psychological outcomes overall at the end of the term.
This is consistent with MTD-based research showing that goal engagement strategies particularly benefit students who face academic barriers (Hamm et al., 2015 (Hamm et al., , 2019)).

text.text: Students in the Low and Medium Strategy profiles, who had performed better on the midterm, did not outperform students in the Engaged Strategy profile in final course grades.
Although these students had rated the course as their most difficult, they may have been performing as well as or better than they expected.

Because students need to distribute limited time and resources across all their courses, maintaining their current approach in the difficult course may reflect efficient distribution of their resources.
Our findings support and extend MTD.
According to the congruence principle, control strategies are adaptive when they match the opportunities and constraints of a situation (Heckhausen et al., 2010 (Heckhausen et al., , 2019)).

text.text: Goal engagement is adaptive when goals remain attainable despite setbacks.

Although we did not measure goals or their attainability directly, the favorable outcomes of the Engaged Strategy profile suggest that these students perceived their goals as still attainable and chose congruent strategies.
Students in this profile may have had the potential to succeed but intensified their effort only after receiving a relatively low midterm grade.
The High Strategy profile is more difficult to interpret.

Combining strategies is not maladaptive per se: goal adjustment can reflect the recalibration of overambitious goals (von Keyserlingk et al., 2022), and self-protection can sustain motivation for continued striving, particularly among struggling students (Hall, Perry, et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Combining strategies is not maladaptive per se: goal adjustment can reflect the recalibration of overambitious goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(von Keyserlingk et al., 2022)</ref>, and self-protection can sustain motivation for continued striving, particularly among struggling students <ref type="bibr">(Hall, Perry, et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Yet students who combined high goal engagement with goal adjustment and self-protection obtained the lowest final course grades and reported more negative feelings, despite also reporting more positive feelings.
One explanation is that these students were uncertain whether their goals were still attainable.

Intending to work harder while lowering one's aspirations and normalizing one's struggles may reflect this uncertainty, and dividing limited resources across strategies may be less effective than investing them in goal engagement.
Moreover, although students in this profile endorsed help-seeking more than students in other profiles, it was among their least endorsed strategies.

These students might have benefited most from support in selecting effective learning strategies, rather than simply investing more time and effort, which can lead to exhaustion without the desired results.
Finally, because students in the High Strategy profile also had the lowest midterm grades, their lower final grades may reflect their ongoing academic struggles.
Our findings have three implications for educational practice.
First, it is important to identify struggling students and provide targeted learning support.
About one third of the students in our sample belonged to the High Strategy profile (24%-42% per quarter), which was associated with the lowest final course grades.
These students may be highly motivated but uncertain about how to respond effectively to academic challenges, illustrating that more effort does not always translate into better outcomes.

Studies using digital trace data similarly show that many students struggle with self-regulated learning and exhibit engagement patterns associated with low performance (Nguyen et al., 2020; Rodriguez et al., 2021; von Keyserlingk et al., 2025).

text.text: Second, institutions should promote campus learning resources and encourage helpseeking.
Students in our sample rarely intended to seek help from academic counselors or the learning assistance center, which may be common in competitive college environments.

Because adaptive help-seeking supports academic persistence and success, instructors and administrators should create contexts that encourage help-seeking (Johnson et al., 2022; Karabenick & Gonida, 2017) and examine potential barriers, such as stigma or a lack of awareness of available resources.

text.text: Finally, support should help students evaluate whether their goals remain attainable and select strategies accordingly.

No profile in our sample combined goal adjustment with low goal engagement, suggesting that students in high-achieving environments rarely consider stepping back from their grade goals, possibly because of institutional or cultural pressures.
Students in the High Strategy profile intended to engage and adjust simultaneously, a combination associated with poorer outcomes.

Interventions should help students reassess goal attainability, select strategies that match their circumstances, and, when necessary, pivot to more attainable goals, which has been linked to higher well-being (Wrosch et al., 2003), rather than simply encouraging all students to work harder.

text.text: One strength of our study is that we used longitudinal data from three student cohorts to investigate profiles, profile predictors, and profile outcomes in up to three difficult courses per student.
We replicated these profiles across three consecutive quarters, demonstrating their robustness.
However, our study has some limitations.
First, our sample consisted of students from a competitive research university, which may explain why no profile combined goal adjustment with low goal engagement.
Future research should examine whether different institutional contexts, such as community colleges or less selective institutions, produce different profile structures.
Second, we measured students' intentions or likelihood of strategy use, rather than implementation, which may not fully capture students' regulatory behavior.
Future studies could employ experience sampling methods or behavioral trace data to assess strategy use in real time.
Moreover, latent transition analysis could reveal whether students shift between profiles as they encounter new setbacks or consistently adopt particular regulatory patterns.
In our sample, too few students participated in all three quarters to conduct such an analysis.
Third, we used the final course grade as the sole academic outcome, without accounting for students' grade expectations, which are key to understanding how students adjust their goals.
Future studies should assess grade expectations alongside performance metrics to provide a more complete picture of profile adaptivity.
Fourth, our psychological well-being survey was a generic, retrospective measure of positive and negative feelings across the quarter.
Although experiences in a very difficult course likely affect overall well-being during a quarter, they do not represent students' entire college experience.
Future studies should therefore assess course-specific emotions at multiple time points to examine how they change in response to performance feedback and control strategy use.
We investigated college students' profiles of intended control strategy use after midterm exams in their most difficult course, as well as the predictors and outcomes of these profiles.

Of the four profiles identified, the Engaged Strategy profile appeared to be the most adaptive response to a setback, as it was associated with higher final course grades and more positive feelings, despite relatively low midterm exam performance.
Combining high goal engagement with goal adjustment and self-protection, in contrast, was associated with the lowest grades and more negative feelings.
These findings are consistent with MTD's proposition that adaptive self-regulation requires strategies that are congruent with the situation.

Educators and advisors should help students assess whether their goals remain attainable, point them to support structures that can improve their learning behaviors and strategies, and pay particular attention to highly motivated students who struggle to choose effective strategies.
Further research should examine these profiles, their predictors, and their adaptivity across institutional contexts and populations.
